title: The Delivery Framework
summary: A 45-minute path from vague prompt to working design, with estimation only where it changes a decision.
keyPoints: Requirements come before components: functional, non-functional, and the top three to five constraints.
Estimate only when a number changes a design decision; you can also estimate later in context.
Name core entities and a small interface before drawing the high-level design.
Keep the first diagram boring and end to end; add components only when a requirement forces them.
Lead one or two deep dives, then invite the interviewer to probe.
Close with the main bottleneck, the trade-offs, and what you would change at 10x.

complexity.note: Write a short in-scope and out-of-scope list.
Smallest diagram that covers the core path.
State the risk before the solution.

commonMistakes: Spending ten minutes on estimation before the design has a decision to inform.
Listing features instead of choosing the three to five requirements that shape the system.
Drawing services and queues before defining the core entities and interface.
Letting the interviewer carry every deep dive without stating your own risks.
interviewNotes: Write requirements where the interviewer can see them and refer back to them.
When a number changes a choice, show the arithmetic; otherwise skip it.
Say why you chose each component and what you would remove at a smaller scale.
If you get stuck, walk one request through the diagram and name the weak point.

checkYourself.question: Why can estimation wait until later in the interview?
checkYourself.answer: An estimate is useful when it informs a decision. If the design choice is clear, a number produced at the start may never affect the architecture.

checkYourself.question: What should the high-level design show before deep dives begin?
checkYourself.answer: One complete flow: where requests enter, where data is written, where it is read, and where it is cached.

checkYourself.question: How do you lead a deep dive without ignoring the interviewer?
checkYourself.answer: State the risk, propose a solution, name the trade-off, and invite the interviewer to choose the next area.
